title: 220,000 Evacuated as France and Spain Burn, Russia Kills 10 at Ukraine Drone Exhibition, ICC Removes Prosecutor Karim Khan
subhead: The largest wildfire evacuations in European history grip France and Spain as Macron mobilises the military, Russia strikes a drone exhibition near Kyiv killing civilians, and the ICC votes out its chief prosecutor — while Pakistan reels from a suicide bombing that killed 27 and Venezuela announces it is quitting the court.

sections.heading: France and Spain Face Record Wildfire Evacuations
sections.body:
More than 220,000 people have been forced from their homes across southern France and northeastern Spain in what officials are calling the largest wildfire evacuation in European history. French President Emmanuel Macron mobilised the military to assist civilian firefighting efforts as blazes tore through Mediterranean coastal zones, fueled by extreme heat and high winds.

According to the BBC, entire tourist resorts and residential areas along the French Riviera and Catalonia's Costa Brava were emptied in scenes reminiscent of a war zone. Firefighters from multiple EU countries have been deployed under the bloc's mutual civil protection mechanism. The fires come amid a summer of record temperatures across the Mediterranean basin.
sections.whyItMatters: A 220,000-person evacuation is unprecedented in Europe and strains EU emergency coordination at a time when the continent is already managing war in Ukraine and energy transition costs. Reconstruction and insurance costs will run into billions.

sections.heading: Russia Hits Ukraine Drone Exhibition, Killing 10
sections.body:
A Russian missile struck a drone technology exhibition near Kyiv on Thursday, killing at least 10 people and wounding around 100, according to the BBC. The exhibition was showcasing Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicle innovations — a sector that has become central to Ukraine's defence strategy under former minister Mykhailo Fedorov.

The attack targeted the very technology that has defined Ukraine's asymmetric warfare approach. It came as President Zelensky continues to grapple with the political fallout from his dismissal of Fedorov as defence minister. According to the BBC, Fedorov has rejected all alternative posts Zelensky offered, saying only the defence ministry, the military command, or the presidency itself would give him real authority. Protesters continue to demonstrate daily in Kyiv demanding Fedorov's reinstatement.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia deliberately targeted Ukraine's drone innovation sector — the one area where Kyiv holds a qualitative edge. Meanwhile, the Fedorov crisis continues to erode Zelensky's domestic standing ahead of a difficult winter.

sections.heading: ICC Removes Prosecutor Karim Khan; Venezuela Quits the Court
sections.body:
The International Criminal Court's assembly voted to remove chief prosecutor Karim Khan, with 82 votes in favour, according to the BBC. Khan had faced allegations of sexual misconduct, and the vote marks the first time the ICC has removed its top prosecutor through the assembly's political process rather than a judicial one.

Hours later, Venezuela announced it would withdraw from the ICC, citing what it called the court's 'geographical bias' against Global South nations. According to Al Jazeera, Venezuela's Foreign Minister Felix Plasencia informed the UN of the 'irrevocable' decision on the orders of interim President Delcy Rodriguez. The move follows US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's pledge last week to 'systematically disable' the ICC, and comes amid the Trump administration's sanctions against ICC prosecutors investigating US and Israeli personnel.
sections.whyItMatters: The ICC is facing a coordinated assault: its prosecutor removed by member states, a member state withdrawing, and the world's most powerful country actively trying to dismantle it. The institution's credibility as a check on impunity is in genuine jeopardy.

sections.heading: Pakistan Car Bomb Kills 27 as Militancy Surges
sections.body:
A suicide car bombing at a security checkpoint in Pakistan's Tank district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, killed 27 people including 12 soldiers, two police officers, and a forestry official, according to Al Jazeera. The Pakistani Taliban (TTP) claimed responsibility, saying four suicide bombers carried out the assault.

The bombing is the latest in an escalating wave of attacks in Pakistan's northwest. According to the Centre for Research and Security Studies, fatalities rose from 1,620 in 2024 to 2,331 last year, while the Pakistan Institute for Peace Studies recorded a 34 percent increase in attacks over the same period. The violence has intensified since the Taliban's return to power in neighbouring Afghanistan, with Pakistan conducting retaliatory air strikes on Afghan soil and the UN documenting hundreds of Afghan civilian deaths from those strikes.
sections.whyItMatters: Pakistan's militancy problem is worsening sharply, with cross-border dimensions that pit two nuclear-armed neighbours against each other. The TTP's boldness signals that the Afghan Taliban's rise has emboldened, not contained, regional armed groups.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Strikes Houthi-Held Hodeidah as Red Sea Crisis Escalates
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia launched strikes on the Houthi-held port city of Hodeidah late Friday, according to the Houthi-controlled Foreign Ministry and Al Jazeera. The attack targeted telecommunications infrastructure and the port area, marking the most direct Saudi-Houthi confrontation since an informal truce took hold in 2022.

The strikes came two days after Houthis targeted Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, damaging at least one, in enforcement of a maritime embargo the group announced on July 20. Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdul Salam said the group's naval operations target only Saudi vessels and do not block the Bab al-Mandab Strait. The Saudi-led coalition vowed to 'take all necessary operational actions' against further Houthi attacks.

Meanwhile, the US-Iran confrontation continued for its 13th consecutive night, with Iran deploying drones against US Middle East facilities and the US firing on a blockade-breaching vessel near Hormuz. The parallel disruptions at Bab al-Mandab and Hormuz now threaten roughly 40 percent of global seaborne oil transit.
sections.whyItMatters: The Saudi-Houthi escalation adds a second front to the Red Sea disruption. With both Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab under threat, global shipping faces the most sustained dual-chokepoint crisis in modern energy market history.

sections.heading: Trump Tariffs Face Court Challenge as US-Canada Rift Deepens Over Bridge
sections.body:
Two US small businesses filed a lawsuit in the US trade court on Friday challenging Trump's new 10-12.5 percent tariffs on 60 trading partners, according to Al Jazeera. The suit argues that Section 301 of the Trade Act — the legal authority invoked — has historically been used for targeted, country-specific actions, not broad-brush tariffs on 60 nations simultaneously. The Liberty Justice Center, which successfully challenged previous IEEPA-based tariffs, is representing the plaintiffs.

The tariffs, imposed Friday, target the EU, UK, China, and others over forced labour allegations, taking effect just as a temporary 10 percent global tariff expired. The US Supreme Court had ruled most of Trump's earlier IEEPA tariffs illegal in February.

In Canada, the $4.7 billion Gordie Howe International Bridge opened without any US officials present, after Canada cancelled a planned cross-border ribbon-cutting ceremony amid Trump's threat to impose 50 percent tariffs on Canada and a dispute over toll revenue sharing. Trump claimed the US would now receive 50 percent of bridge profits. Canadian PM Mark Carney countered that no toll splitting would occur until Canada recouped its construction costs, though a newly released draft agreement showed a 50-50 revenue split for the first 15 years with no repayment provision.
sections.whyItMatters: Trump's tariff regime faces its most serious legal challenge yet, from the same lawyers who already won at the Supreme Court once. Meanwhile, the spectacle of a binational bridge opening without one nation's officials shows how far US-Canada relations have deteriorated.

bottomLine: A day defined by fire and fracture. Europe faces its worst wildfire crisis in recorded history with 220,000 displaced, while Russia deliberately targeted Ukraine's drone innovation sector and the ICC lost its prosecutor to a political removal vote — hours before Venezuela walked out of the court entirely. Pakistan's militancy surge killed 27 at a checkpoint, and Saudi Arabia broke a four-year truce by striking Hodeidah, adding a second front to the Red Sea disruption that already has global oil markets on edge. Trump's new tariffs on 60 nations face immediate legal challenge, and even a bridge opening between allies became a diplomatic incident.
